summary: Gives recommendations for filtering ICMPv6 messages in firewalls. ICMPv6 is essential for IPv6 to work but has many message types and options, and letting everything through has security risks. The memo suggests what to allow and what to block. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 relies on ICMPv6 messages for errors, discovery, and other network functions. RFC 4890 explains which messages firewalls should pass, which they can filter by policy, and which they should generally block.

subtitle: How firewalls can filter ICMPv6 without breaking functions that IPv6 needs.

tldr.problem: ICMPv6 performs functions that IPv6 needs, but unrestricted forwarding can create security risks. Filtering habits from IPv4 can also break IPv6 communication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts ICMPv6 messages into categories for transit traffic and traffic addressed to the firewall, with recommendations based on message type, address scope, and firewall role.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4890 is an Informational set of firewall recommendations. It aims to preserve needed IPv6 communication while allowing administrators to apply local policy to other messages.

today: RFC 4890 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document's examples refer to the specifications available when it was written.

sections.title: Why ICMPv6 Filtering Matters
sections.content:
ICMPv6 supports error reporting, connectivity checks, neighbor and router discovery, address configuration, path MTU discovery, multicast functions, and mobility. Dropping too many messages can prevent IPv6 communication from starting or continuing, while passing all messages without controls can expose a site to security risks.

The right rules depend in part on whether a firewall protects an individual host, an end site, or a transit site. The RFC generally advises Internet service providers not to filter ICMPv6 messages that transit their sites, leaving end sites to apply their own policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Some ICMPv6 messages are required for IPv6 to work, while others may create risks. Firewall rules need to consider what each message does and where it is going.

sections.title: Message Types, Scope, and Destination
sections.content:
The ICMPv6 Type field is eight bits. Types at or below 127 are error messages; higher types are informational messages. A firewall also needs to consider whether a message is for communication across the Internet, can come from any point along the path, or is limited to one local link.

Address type and scope matter as much as the ICMPv6 type. Many local messages are not forwarded by IPv6 routers, and receivers check conditions such as a hop limit of 255 or a link-local source address. A bridge is different from a router: it joins two physical links into one logical link, so local discovery messages may need to cross it.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall should check both the message type and the source and destination addresses. Messages intended only for one local link should not be forwarded by a router.

sections.title: Threats the Rules Address
sections.content:
The RFC discusses denial of service, probing, redirection, renumbering attacks, and covert communication through ICMPv6 error messages. Many useful messages cannot be authenticated with IPsec because a site may need to accept them from sources across the Internet.

Filtering therefore provides an important defense, but it must preserve the messages required for communication. For example, a malicious Redirect can divert packets, and error messages can carry hidden traffic; the RFC discusses address checks and inspection of the packet embedded in an error message as possible safeguards.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers may use ICMPv6 to disrupt connections, learn about hosts, redirect traffic, or carry hidden data. Firewalls reduce these risks but cannot simply block every message.

sections.title: Filtering Transit Traffic
sections.content:
For traffic crossing an end-site firewall, the RFC says not to drop Destination Unreachable (Type 1), Packet Too Big (Type 2), Time Exceeded (Type 3, Code 0), Parameter Problem (Type 4, Codes 1 and 2), Echo Request (Type 128), or Echo Response (Type 129). It says Time Exceeded Code 1, Parameter Problem Code 0, and Mobile IPv6 message Types 144 through 147 normally should not be dropped.

Neighbor and router discovery, multicast listener discovery, SEND certificate-path messages, and multicast-router discovery are link-local and are normally dropped by routers or rejected by receivers. A firewall should define policy for Seamoby Experimental Type 150 and unallocated types. The RFC recommends dropping Node Information Types 139 and 140, Router Renumbering Type 138, experimental Types 100, 101, 200, and 201, and extension Types 127 and 255 unless there is a good reason to allow them.
sections.plainLanguage: Several error messages and echo messages should pass through a site firewall. Many discovery messages stay on the local link, while experimental and information-query messages need explicit policy.

sections.title: Messages Addressed to the Firewall
sections.content:
A firewall must also receive messages addressed to its own interfaces. The RFC says not to drop the essential error and echo messages or the router, neighbor, inverse-neighbor, multicast-listener, SEND certificate-path, and multicast-router discovery messages needed to configure and maintain IPv6 communication.

Redirect messages need a policy decision because they can create security risks. Node Information messages also need a local decision if the service is enabled. Mobile IPv6 and experimental messages may be dropped when the firewall does not provide the corresponding service. Rules may differ between private and public interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall must accept messages it needs to configure its own IPv6 interfaces and communicate with neighbors. Administrators can set policy for Redirect and optional services on each interface.
